name: Infraorbital rim / zygomatic filler

lead: Infraorbital rim and zygomatic filler uses injectable gel, usually hyaluronic acid, to add volume under the eye and over the cheekbone for a more supported look.
Evidence consists of small pilot studies, anatomical studies and complication reviews; no large trials were found.

paras: Filler is injected into the tissue around the orbital rim and cheek to add volume and projection. Researchers are studying depth, vessel locations and fat patterns to refine placement [3][5][6].

Common effects are bruising, swelling, blue-grey tint and contour irregularities [2]. Rarely, filler entering an artery can cause tissue death or permanent vision loss [1]. Fillers are regulated as medical devices in the US [1].

lead: Infraorbital rim and zygomatic filler refers to injectable fillers, usually hyaluronic acid, placed around the lower orbital rim and cheekbone to add apparent support under the eye. Wikipedia describes injectable fillers as materials used to smooth wrinkles, restore volume and contour areas such as the cheeks [1]. In appearance communities the aim is often described as building skeletal-looking support for a deeper-set, more supported eye region.

The infraorbital area is anatomically delicate. Reviews list bruising, malar oedema, blue-grey discolouration and contour irregularities as common complications, with uncommon serious events [2]. Small pilot and cadaver studies have examined placement and behaviour of hyaluronic acid in the region [3][4].
infobox: Fillers are regulated as medical devices in the US [1]
Bruising, oedema, discolouration, rare vascular occlusion [1][2]

paras: Most hyaluronic acid fillers are chemically crosslinked, commonly with BDDE, to improve durability [1]. Infraorbital filler is used for tear trough and under-eye hollows; a 2024 paper notes ongoing debate about injection practice, placement depth and filler behaviour in this region [3].

A 2020 review lists ecchymosis, malar oedema, blue-grey hue and contour irregularities as the most common complications of infraorbital filler [2]. Wikipedia reports that, rarely, filler can enter an artery and cause vascular occlusion, potentially leading to permanent vision loss or skin necrosis [1]. A 2024 CT study of 84 hemifacial specimens mapped infraorbital vasculature to inform safer injection [5], and a 2026 ultrasound study classified infraorbital fat and groove patterns, noting that placement into fat can cause bulging [6].

Small human and cadaver studies exist. A multimodal pilot study combined patient injections of a hyaluronic acid filler with 3D imaging, patient-reported outcomes and cadaveric assessment [3]. A completed registered study of infraorbital filler enrolled 11 participants [7], and a larger registry of real-life facial filler use (n=460) is recruiting [8]. Large controlled trials specific to rim or zygomatic augmentation for skeletal support were not found.
